analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from hiring permanent strikebreaker workers during the first ten weeks of a strike.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 100 House cosponsors, never left committee and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer may permanently replace workers who go on strike over wages or conditions. This bill would change that: for the first ten weeks of any strike, an employer could not hire, threaten to hire, or arrange to hire permanent replacements for striking workers. Strikers could keep picketing for ten weeks knowing their jobs would be waiting. The bill was introduced in March 1989, referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, and sent to a subcommittee. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a vote on the House floor, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who strike, and the unions that represent them. Today, an employer can end an economic strike by permanently replacing the strikers, which means workers who exercise their legal right to strike risk losing their jobs for good. Under this bill, striking workers would keep their jobs for at least ten weeks, giving unions real leverage to win better wages and conditions without the fear of permanent job loss. Strikers at companies like the ones where permanent replacements were famously used would have kept their jobs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it an unfair labor practice — a violation of federal law enforceable by the National Labor Relations Board — for an employer to hire, threaten to hire, or contract for permanent replacement workers during the first ten weeks of any strike, whether the strike is over working conditions or over economics [S2] [S3].

The ban applies to the ten-week period beginning on the day the strike starts, and it covers any offer of permanent employment as a replacement for employees on strike, so strikers would know their jobs could not be permanently filled during that window [S3].
The change would take effect for strikes beginning on or after enactment, so it would immediately apply to new disputes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially companies facing strikes, would bear the cost. Today, the ability to permanently replace strikers is an employer's main counterweight to a strike; removing it for ten weeks would force employers to keep positions open, absorb lost production, or settle with the union on its terms. Businesses and management-side groups have long argued that permanent replacement is a lawful, necessary balance to union strike power, and that eliminating it would raise the cost of doing business and invite more strikes.

drawbacks.text: Employers argue that the right to permanently replace economic strikers is the legal counterbalance that keeps strikes limited and manageable; removing it for ten weeks would tilt that balance sharply toward unions, potentially encouraging more strikes and leaving companies unable to keep supplying customers [S2] [S3].

A ten-week moratorium is a blunt tool: it applies equally to a company on the edge of bankruptcy and to a highly profitable one, and it does not address longer strikes, where the risk of permanent replacement would still hang over workers after week ten [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For striking workers, the benefit is concrete: ten weeks of knowing their jobs cannot be permanently filled, which makes striking a survivable choice rather than a gamble with their livelihood. The cost falls on employers, who lose their strongest lever for ending a strike, and some of that cost would be passed to consumers through higher prices or lost production. Honest observers on the business side consider the current replacement right essential to balanced labor law; honest supporters consider it a tool that lets employers erase the right to strike. The bill addresses a real imbalance for workers, but only partially, since it expires at week ten.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Education and Labor Committee and its subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress; it was never given a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Brennan of Maine introduced the bill on March 14, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1] [S5].
Three weeks later, on April 5, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where no further action was recorded [S5].

The bill attracted 100 cosponsors, 97 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but that support was never converted into any vote in committee or on the floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on the ability to permanently replace striking workers are better off, because the ten-week ban never became law and the existing rules remained untouched. The House committee leadership, which controlled whether the bill advanced, faced no consequence for letting it expire.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 97 of 257 House Democrats versus 3 of 175 House Republicans — though the bill drew a handful of Republican backers and never reached a vote that would have tested the chambers' party split.

industries.industry: Employers facing strikes (manufacturing, airlines, and other unionized industries)
industries.note: The bill would take away their ability to permanently replace strikers for ten weeks, a lever they use to keep operating and to pressure unions to settle. Industry groups have long defended the practice as a lawful balance to union strike power.

Firms that supply replacement workers during labor disputes would lose the part of their business built on permanent strikebreaker placements during the first ten weeks of a strike. Temporary staffing during the window would remain possible, but not permanent offers.

Unions would gain leverage in negotiations, since members could strike for ten weeks without risking permanent job loss. That leverage exists to win better pay and conditions for the same workers the bill protects.
